question.worked_solution:
First, note that the series can be written as

$$
\frac{4}{3}{\sum }_{n=5}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n(n+1)}.
$$

Using partial fractions we can write the series as

$$
\frac{4}{3}{\sum }_{n=5}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}).
$$

Computing the first few partial sums, starting with $n=5,$ gives

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{5} & =\frac{4}{3}[(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{6})] \\ {s}_{6} & =\frac{4}{3}[(\frac{1}{5}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\frac{1}{7})] \\ {s}_{7} & =\frac{4}{3}[(\frac{1}{5}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{7}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{7}}-\frac{1}{8})] \\ {s}_{8} & =\frac{4}{3}[(\frac{1}{5}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{7}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{7}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{8}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{8}}-\frac{1}{9})].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms with the exception of the first and last terms. Therefore, the $N$th partial sum is

$$
{s}_{N}=\frac{4}{3}[\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{N+1}].
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by taking the limit of ${s}_{N}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=5}^{\infty }\frac{4}{3n(n+1)} & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }{s}_{N} \\  & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }\frac{4}{3}[\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{N+1}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[\frac{1}{5}-0] \\  & =\frac{4}{15}\end{aligned}
$$
